interactions.label: In India, breast cancer is the most common cancer in females in both urban and r

params.question: In India, breast cancer is the most common cancer in females in both urban and rural regions.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect. The narration distinguishes two patterns: breast cancer leads in urban areas, while cervical cancer dominates in rural India. Recognising this divide is essential for planning region-appropriate screening — mammography in cities, VIA or Pap smears in rural districts.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. While breast cancer leads in urban India, cervical cancer dominates in rural regions. This urban–rural divide reflects differences in screening access, HPV exposure, and reproductive health services — and determines which screening programme a district should prioritise.

params.question: A 58-year-old man presents with progressive dysphagia. He has smoked 10 cigarettes daily for 30 years. What is his tobacco exposure in pack-years?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. 10 is simply the number of cigarettes per day. Pack-years are calculated as (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years smoked, giving (10 ÷ 20) × 30 = 15 pack-years.
Correct. Pack-years = (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years smoked = (10 ÷ 20) × 30 = 15. This standardised measure allows you to stratify cancer risk and compare exposure across patients.
Incorrect. Apply the formula: (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years smoked = (10 ÷ 20) × 30 = 15 pack-years, not 20.
Incorrect. 30 is the number of years smoked, not the pack-year value. The formula divides daily cigarettes by 20 first: (10 ÷ 20) × 30 = 15 pack-years.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the pack-year formula: (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years smoked. Here: (10 ÷ 20) × 30 = 15. This standardised measure is used in every oncological history.
Well done. Quantifying tobacco exposure in pack-years is essential — it stratifies lung, laryngeal, and oesophageal cancer risk and guides screening decisions.

interactions.label: A 55-year-old man is referred for prostate cancer evaluation. You plan to perfor

params.question: A 55-year-old man is referred for prostate cancer evaluation. You plan to perform both a PSA blood test and a digital rectal examination. Which sequence is correct, and why?

answers.text: Perform DRE first, then draw PSA — the examination primes the prostate for a more accurate reading

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. DRE does not improve PSA accuracy. Mechanical manipulation of the prostate transiently raises PSA, producing a falsely elevated result if blood is drawn afterwards.

answers.text: Draw PSA first, then perform DRE — the procedure can transiently raise PSA levels

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. DRE can transiently elevate PSA through mechanical manipulation of the prostate. Drawing blood first avoids this confounder, ensuring the PSA value reflects the true baseline.

answers.text: Either order is acceptable — DRE does not affect PSA values

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Order matters. DRE can transiently raise PSA, which may push a borderline value into the abnormal range and trigger unnecessary further investigation.

answers.text: PSA alone is sufficient — DRE adds no clinical information to the assessment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. DRE provides complementary information: it detects nodularity, asymmetry, or induration that PSA alone may miss. Both are part of a complete prostate evaluation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: DRE transiently raises PSA. Always draw blood for PSA before performing the rectal examination to avoid a falsely elevated result.
Exactly. Drawing PSA before DRE avoids a transient artefactual rise — a simple sequencing step that prevents unnecessary biopsies.

interactions.label: A 65-year-old woman with metastatic colorectal cancer has an ECOG performance st

params.question: A 65-year-old woman with metastatic colorectal cancer has an ECOG performance status of 1. She wishes to remain active with her grandchildren for as long as possible and understands cure is not achievable. Which treatment approach best aligns with her stated values?

answers.text: Aggressive curative-intent combination chemotherapy to attempt complete remission

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. With confirmed metastatic disease, cure is not feasible. Pursuing aggressive curative-intent treatment would increase toxicity without achieving her goal of maintaining functional status.

answers.text: Palliative chemotherapy to extend functional survival while maintaining quality of life

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Palliative chemotherapy in metastatic colorectal cancer can extend survival while keeping the patient functional — directly matching her goal. Treatment intent must align with what the patient values, not just what the disease permits.

answers.text: Immediate hospice enrolment with cessation of all anti-cancer treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. With ECOG 1, this patient retains good functional status and can benefit from palliative chemotherapy. Hospice is appropriate later, when active treatment no longer serves her goals.

answers.text: Surgical resection of the primary tumour alone, without systemic therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Surgery alone does not address metastatic deposits. A systemic palliative approach guided by her preference for maintained function is more appropriate.

overallFeedback.feedback: In metastatic disease, the choice between curative and palliative intent is driven by biology and patient values together. Here, with ECOG 1 and a goal of functional survival, palliative chemotherapy is the best fit.
Well done. Matching treatment intent to patient values is the core of shared decision-making — the tumour board provides options, but the patient's goals set the direction.

interactions.label: A terminally ill cancer patient has a documented advance directive refusing mech

params.question: A terminally ill cancer patient has a documented advance directive refusing mechanical ventilation. The family insists on intubation. Under the 2018 Common Cause versus Union of India judgment, which course of action is legally correct?

answers.text: Follow the family's wishes, as next of kin have overriding legal authority in end-of-life decisions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While family input is valued, the Supreme Court judgment affirms the patient's advance directive as legally valid. Patient autonomy under Article 21 takes precedence over family preference.

answers.text: Honour the advance directive, as it is legally valid and dying with dignity is a right under Article 21

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Common Cause judgment established that advance directives are legally binding and that dying with dignity is a fundamental right under Article 21. The patient's documented wishes govern, even when the family disagrees.

answers.text: Defer to the hospital ethics committee before taking any action, as the advance directive requires committee ratification

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A valid advance directive has direct legal standing under the 2018 judgment. While ethics committees play an advisory role, committee ratification is not required to honour the patient's documented wishes.

answers.text: Proceed with intubation, because withholding ventilation from a living patient constitutes active euthanasia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Withholding unwanted treatment in accordance with an advance directive is passive euthanasia, which is lawful under the judgment. Active euthanasia — such as administering a lethal agent — remains illegal in India.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the Common Cause judgment: advance directives are legally valid, dying with dignity is a right under Article 21, passive euthanasia is lawful, and active euthanasia remains illegal.
Exactly. The 2018 Supreme Court judgment makes advance directives legally binding. Respecting the patient's autonomy is not just ethical — it is the law.
